statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline F_q, let d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), and let F_u be the unipotent part of F. Then beta(F_u x,F_u y)=beta(x,y) for all x,y in H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell).
proof:
Let q=p^a, ell != p, m>=1, k=overline(F_q), d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Put V = H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell), and let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on V, i.e. F = (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}. Let beta: V x V -> Q_ell be the Poincare duality pairing, i.e. beta(x,y) = tr(x cup y) where tr: H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> Q_ell(-d) is the normalized Poincare duality trace tr(cl(z))=[k(z):F_{q^m}], composed with the fixed identification Q_ell(-d) ~ Q_ell given by the chosen nonzero element of Q_ell(1). Let F_u be the unipotent part of F in its multiplicative Jordan decomposition in GL(V). We must prove beta(F_u x, F_u y) = beta(x,y) for all x,y in V.

Step 1 (F is a similitude of beta with multiplier q^{md}). Apply lemma_77 (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77) with Y = X. Its part (b) says that for every n with 0<=n<=2d the pairing H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) x H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell(-d), (x,y) |-> tr(x cup y), is a perfect pairing of Q_ell-vector spaces and satisfies <Fx,Fy> = q^{md}<x,y> for all x,y. Taking n = d gives exactly that our pairing beta (before the Tate-twist identification, with values in Q_ell(-d)) is perfect and satisfies <Fx,Fy> = q^{md}<x,y> for all x,y in V. Composing with the fixed Q_ell-linear isomorphism Q_ell(-d) ~ Q_ell (which is just scalar multiplication by the chosen nonzero element of Q_ell(1), a Q_ell-linear change of coordinates on the target) preserves both perfectness and the similitude identity, so beta is a perfect Q_ell-bilinear form on V and
  beta(Fx, Fy) = q^{md} beta(x,y)   for all x,y in V.

Step 2 (F is invertible). F is the pullback on etale cohomology of the automorphism (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma) of X_k (lemma_77 refers to F precisely as the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of X_k). Since pullback by an automorphism is an isomorphism (its inverse is the pullback by the inverse automorphism), F is an invertible Q_ell-linear endomorphism of V, i.e. F in GL(V). Note that V is finite-dimensional: the perfectness of the pairing beta in Step 1 forces V to be finite-dimensional (a perfect pairing against a vector space of the same underlying set identifies V with a quotient of its dual, and the standard finite-dimensionality of etale cohomology of a smooth projective variety over a finite field is the content used in lemma_77, where the pairing is declared perfect).

Step 3 (apply the linear algebra lemma). The field K = Q_ell has characteristic 0. We have a finite-dimensional K-vector space V, a perfect K-bilinear form beta on V (not assumed symmetric or alternating), a scalar c = q^{md} in K^x (a positive rational number, hence nonzero in Q_ell), and T = F in GL_K(V) satisfying <Tv,Tw> = c<v,w> for all v,w in V by Step 1. By lemma_495 (Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_495), if T = T_s T_u = T_u T_s is the multiplicative Jordan decomposition of T, then T_s and T_u are again similitudes of the form, with multipliers c and 1 respectively; in particular
  <T_u v, T_u w> = <v,w>   for all v,w in V.

Taking T = F, so that T_u = F_u is exactly the unipotent part of F named in the statement, we obtain beta(F_u x, F_u y) = beta(x,y) for all x,y in V = H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell), which is the desired conclusion. No semisimplicity of F was used anywhere; the argument uses only the Frobenius-equivariance of Poincare duality (lemma_77) and the linear algebra fact of lemma_495.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline F_q, let d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, put P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) preserving P^d, let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), set G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+(-1)^d q^{md} beta(x,F^{-1}y) on P^d, and let U be the unipotent part of F|_{P^d}. If G is symmetric and anisotropic and U is a G-isometry, then F is semisimple on P^d.
proof:
I have everything I need. The target lemma is a pure linear-algebra statement: the cohomological data (X, ξ, L, P^d, F, β, G) merely defines the objects, and the three hypotheses (G symmetric, G anisotropic, U a G-isometry) together with "U unipotent" feed directly into `Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_520`, which concludes U = id. Since F|_{P^d} = F_s·U with F_s semisimple, U = id makes F|_{P^d} semisimple.

Let me confirm each hypothesis of lemma_520 against the target:
- K = Q_ℓ has characteristic 0 (ℓ is prime) ✓
- V = P^d is a finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector space (a subspace of finite-dimensional étale cohomology) ✓
- B = G is symmetric (hypothesis) ✓
- B(v,v) ≠ 0 for every nonzero v (this is exactly "G is anisotropic") ✓
- U is unipotent (it is the unipotent part of F|_{P^d}) ✓
- U is a B-isometry (hypothesis) ✓

All conditions hold, so U = id, i.e. F is semisimple on P^d.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline F_q, let d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), and set G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+(-1)^d q^{md} beta(x,F^{-1}y). Then G(x,y)=G(y,x) for all x,y in H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell).
proof: Let V = H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) and put C = q^{md}. All scalar computations take place in Q_ell after the fixed identification of Tate twists with Q_ell; the rational scalar C is unaffected by this identification. We use the Q_ell-valued Poincare duality pairing obtained from the normalized trace in eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77; the symmetry to be proved is unchanged if beta is replaced by any nonzero scalar multiple. By part (b) of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 with n = d, for all u,v in V one has beta(Fu,Fv) = C beta(u,v). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, applied with the prime power q^m in place of q, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F is an automorphism of V, so F^{-1} exists and F(F^{-1}w) = w for every w in V. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_469, applied with the prime power q^m in place of q and with n = d, the normalized Poincare duality pairing satisfies beta(u,v) = (-1)^{d(2d-d)} beta(v,u) = (-1)^d beta(v,u) for all u,v in V. Since C is a nonzero element of Q_ell, C^{-1} exists. Now take arbitrary x,y in V. First, beta(Fx,y) = beta(Fx,F(F^{-1}y)) = C beta(x,F^{-1}y). Second, beta(x,Fy) = beta(F(F^{-1}x),Fy) = C beta(F^{-1}x,y), hence beta(F^{-1}x,y) = C^{-1} beta(x,Fy). Using the sign relation, G(y,x) = beta(y,Fx) + (-1)^d C beta(y,F^{-1}x) = (-1)^d beta(Fx,y) + (-1)^d C (-1)^d beta(F^{-1}x,y) = (-1)^d beta(Fx,y) + C beta(F^{-1}x,y) = (-1)^d C beta(x,F^{-1}y) + C C^{-1} beta(x,Fy) = (-1)^d C beta(x,F^{-1}y) + beta(x,Fy) = G(x,y). Thus G is symmetric.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline F_q, let d>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell), let F_u be the unipotent part of F, and set G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+(-1)^d q^{md} beta(x,F^{-1}y). Then G(F_u x,F_u y)=G(x,y) for all x,y in H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell).
proof:
Set c=q^{md} and \varepsilon=(-1)^d. Let V=H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Poincare duality gives a nondegenerate bilinear pairing  eta:V	imes V	o \mathbb Q_\ell after the fixed identification of Tate twists with \mathbb Q_\ell. The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is pullback by an isomorphism, so F is invertible. By the standard top-degree Frobenius computation (with the trace map normalized by closed points), F acts on H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) by c. Hence, for all a,b\in V,  eta(Fa,Fb)=\operatorname{tr}(F(a\cup b))=c\operatorname{tr}(a\cup b)=c eta(a,b). Since F is invertible, this is equivalent to  eta(Fa,b)=c eta(a,F^{-1}b) for all a,b; in other words, the  eta-adjoint F^{\dagger} of F satisfies F^{\dagger}=cF^{-1}. Work over K=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell and write V_K=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K again as V. By Jordan-Chevalley, F=F_sF_u with F_s semisimple, F_u unipotent, and F_sF_u=F_uF_s; the scalar extension of the given F_u is F_u\otimes 1. Let V= igoplus_{\lambda\in K^*}V_\lambda be the generalized eigenspace decomposition of F. Since F_u commutes with F, it preserves each V_\lambda. On V_\lambda the semisimple part F_s is \lambda I, so F=\lambda F_u there, and F_u|_{V_\lambda} is unipotent, hence invertible. First note that if \lambda,\mu\in K^* and \mu
e c/\lambda, then  eta(V_\lambda,V_\mu)=0. Choose r such that (F-\lambda I)^r kills V_\lambda. For x\in V_\lambda and any z, 0= eta((F-\lambda I)^r x,z)= eta(x,(F^{\dagger}-\lambda I)^r z), because the  eta-adjoint of (F-\lambda I)^r is (F^{\dagger}-\lambda I)^r. On V_\mu, F^{\dagger}=cF^{-1} has generalized eigenvalue c/\mu: indeed, if (F-\mu I)^s z=0, then (F^{-1}-\mu^{-1}I)^s z=(-\mu^{-1})^sF^{-s}(F-\mu I)^s z=0. Since c/\mu
e \lambda, the operator (F^{\dagger}-\lambda I)^r is invertible on V_\mu. Therefore every element of V_\mu is of the form (F^{\dagger}-\lambda I)^r z with z\in V_\mu, and is orthogonal to x. This proves the claim. Now let x\in V_\lambda and z\in V_{c/\lambda}. On V_{c/\lambda} we have F^{-1}=(\lambda/c)F_u^{-1}. Using the adjoint relation  eta(Fx,z)= eta(x,F^{\dagger}z), we obtain \lambda eta(F_u x,z)= eta(Fx,z)= eta(x,cF^{-1}z)=c eta(x,(\lambda/c)F_u^{-1}z)=\lambda eta(x,F_u^{-1}z). Since \lambda
e0,  eta(F_u x,z)= eta(x,F_u^{-1}z). For x\in V_\lambda and y\in V_{c/\lambda}, the identities Fy=(c/\lambda)F_u y and F^{-1}y=(\lambda/c)F_u^{-1}y give G(x,y)=(c/\lambda) eta(x,F_u y)+\varepsilon c(\lambda/c) eta(x,F_u^{-1}y)=(c/\lambda) eta(x,F_u y)+\varepsilon\lambda eta(x,F_u^{-1}y). On the other hand, F(F_u y)=(c/\lambda)F_u^2 y and F^{-1}(F_u y)=(\lambda/c)y, because F and F_u commute. Hence G(F_u x,F_u y)=(c/\lambda) eta(F_u x,F_u^2 y)+\varepsilon\lambda eta(F_u x,y). Applying the relation above with z=F_u^2 y and with z=y gives  eta(F_u x,F_u^2 y)= eta(x,F_u y) and  eta(F_u x,y)= eta(x,F_u^{-1}y). Therefore G(F_u x,F_u y)=G(x,y). Finally let x,y be arbitrary elements of V. Write x=\sum_i x_i and y=\sum_j y_j with x_i\in V_{\lambda_i} and y_j\in V_{\mu_j}; the sums are finite because V_K is finite-dimensional. If \mu_j
e c/\lambda_i, then Fy_j and F^{-1}y_j lie in V_{\mu_j}, so by orthogonality  eta(x_i,Fy_j)= eta(x_i,F^{-1}y_j)=0 and hence G(x_i,y_j)=0; the same vanishing holds for G(F_u x_i,F_u y_j). For the remaining terms, with \mu_j=c/\lambda_i, the computation above gives G(F_u x_i,F_u y_j)=G(x_i,y_j). Summing over i and j yields G(F_u x,F_u y)=G(x,y) over K. In particular it holds for x,y in the original \mathbb Q_\ell-subspace. This proves G(F_u x,F_u y)=G(x,y) for all x,y\in H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

statement: Let K be a field, let H be a finite-dimensional K-vector space with a perfect bilinear pairing ( , ), and let F be a K-linear endomorphism of H. Put V=H⊕H and define the perfect bilinear form on V by ⟨(x,y),(x',y')⟩=(x,y')+(y,x'). Let F_V=F⊕F. For every b∈K[F], let a=b⊕b. If b^† is the adjoint of b with respect to ( , ) on H and a^† is the adjoint of a with respect to ⟨ , ⟩ on V, then Tr_V(aa^†)=2Tr_H(bb^†).
proof:
We prove Tr_V(a a^dagger) = 2 Tr_H(b b^dagger) in three steps: (1) the cross pairing <,> on V is perfect; (2) the adjoint of a = b⊕b with respect to <,> is a^dagger = b^dagger⊕b^dagger; (3) the trace identity follows from the block-diagonal form of a a^dagger.

Step 1: <,> is perfect. The pairing ( , ) on H is perfect, i.e. the map θ_H: H -> H^*, θ_H(t) = (·, t), is an isomorphism. Hence the Gram matrix of ( , ) (with respect to any basis) is invertible, so ( , ) is nondegenerate in each variable: if (x, s) = 0 for every s in H then x = 0 (left nondegeneracy), and if (s, y) = 0 for every s in H then y = 0 (right nondegeneracy).

Now consider θ_V: V -> V^*, θ_V(v) = <v, ·>. We show θ_V is injective; since dim_K V < ∞, θ_V is then an isomorphism, i.e. <,> is perfect. Let v = (x, y) in V with θ_V(v) = 0. Then <v, w> = 0 for every w = (x', y') in V, i.e.
    (x, y') + (y, x') = 0   for all x', y' in H.
Setting x' = 0 gives (x, y') = 0 for all y' in H, so by left nondegeneracy x = 0. Setting y' = 0 gives (y, x') = 0 for all x' in H, so by right nondegeneracy y = 0. Hence v = 0 and θ_V is injective, so <,> is perfect. In particular every endomorphism of V, in particular a, has a unique adjoint.

Step 2: a^dagger = b^dagger ⊕ b^dagger. Recall the defining property of b^dagger on H: for all u, s in H,
    (b·u, s) = (u, b^dagger·s).      (*)
We claim b^dagger⊕b^dagger satisfies the defining property of the adjoint of a on V. Let v = (x, y) in V and w = (x', y') in V. Since a = b⊕b, a v = (b x, b y). Hence
    <a v, w> = <(b x, b y), (x', y')> = (b x, y') + (b y, x').
Apply (*) with u = x and s = y' to get (b x, y') = (x, b^dagger y'), and apply (*) with u = y and s = x' to get (b y, x') = (y, b^dagger x'). Substituting,
    <a v, w> = (x, b^dagger y') + (y, b^dagger x').
On the other hand, (b^dagger⊕b^dagger) w = (b^dagger x', b^dagger y'), so
    <v, (b^dagger⊕b^dagger) w> = <(x, y), (b^dagger x', b^dagger y')> = (x, b^dagger y') + (y, b^dagger x').
Comparing the two expressions gives <a v, w> = <v, (b^dagger⊕b^dagger) w> for all v, w in V. By the uniqueness of the adjoint (guaranteed by the perfectness of <,> from Step 1), a^dagger = b^dagger⊕b^dagger.

Step 3: The trace identity. Using a^dagger = b^dagger⊕b^dagger and that the product of two block-diagonal endomorphisms is block-diagonal with the products of the corresponding blocks,
    a a^dagger = (b⊕b)(b^dagger⊕b^dagger) = (b b^dagger) ⊕ (b b^dagger).
For endomorphisms T_1, T_2 in End_K(H), the trace of T_1⊕T_2 on H⊕H equals Tr_H(T_1) + Tr_H(T_2): choosing a basis of H and using it for both summands makes the matrix of T_1⊕T_2 block-diagonal with diagonal blocks [T_1] and [T_2], whose trace is the sum of the two block traces. Applying this with T_1 = T_2 = b b^dagger,
    Tr_V(a a^dagger) = Tr_H(b b^dagger) + Tr_H(b b^dagger) = 2 Tr_H(b b^dagger).
This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be either 1 or -1, let beta: V x V -> K be a bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let F be an element of GL_K(V), let c be a nonzero element of K, and suppose beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. Put G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+epsilon c beta(x,F^(-1)y). Then G(x,y)=G(y,x) for all x,y in V.
proof: Let x,y be arbitrary elements of V. First record two consequences of the hypotheses. Because beta is epsilon-symmetric, beta(a,b)=epsilon beta(b,a) for all a,b in V, and since epsilon is 1 or -1 we have epsilon^2=1. Also c is nonzero, so c^{-1} exists in K. From beta(Fa,Fb)=c beta(a,b) we obtain, by taking a=x and b=F^{-1}y, that beta(Fx,y)=beta(Fx,F(F^{-1}y))=c beta(x,F^{-1}y). Similarly, taking a=F^{-1}x and b=y gives beta(x,Fy)=beta(F(F^{-1}x),Fy)=c beta(F^{-1}x,y), hence beta(F^{-1}x,y)=c^{-1} beta(x,Fy). Now compute G(y,x). By epsilon-symmetry, beta(y,Fx)=epsilon beta(Fx,y) and beta(y,F^{-1}x)=epsilon beta(F^{-1}x,y). Therefore G(y,x)=epsilon beta(Fx,y)+epsilon c epsilon beta(F^{-1}x,y). Substituting the two identities gives G(y,x)=epsilon c beta(x,F^{-1}y)+epsilon c epsilon c^{-1} beta(x,Fy). Since epsilon^2=1 and c c^{-1}=1, this equals epsilon c beta(x,F^{-1}y)+beta(x,Fy). Addition in K is commutative, so this is beta(x,Fy)+epsilon c beta(x,F^{-1}y)=G(x,y). Thus G(x,y)=G(y,x) for all x,y in V.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, and put k=algebraic closure of F_q. Let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample Cartier divisor, let L be cup product with xi, put P^2=ker(L:H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell)->H^4_et(S_k,Q_ell)). Let tr_S:H^4_et(S_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell be the Poincare duality trace normalized by tr_S(cl(z))=[kappa(z):F_{q^m}] for closed points z, and put beta(x,y)=tr_S(x cup y). If x in P^2 is a nonzero Q-linear combination of the cycle classes of F_{q^m}-rational Cartier divisors on S, then beta(x,x) is a negative rational number.
proof: Let H be the F_{q^m}-rational very ample Cartier divisor whose cycle class is ξ. Write Div_Q(S) for the Q-vector space of Q-Cartier divisors on S. By the hypothesis on x, there is a Q-divisor D = sum_i a_i D_i, with a_i in Q and each D_i an F_{q^m}-rational Cartier divisor, such that x = cl(D). The cycle class map is Q-linear. For Q-divisors D,E on S, the cup product cl(D) cup cl(E) is the cycle class of the intersection 0-cycle D·E (with rational coefficients); for integral divisors meeting properly this is the definition of the cup product of cycle classes, and the general case follows by bilinearity and the standard definition of the intersection product. Under the fixed identification Q_ℓ(2) ≅ Q_ℓ, the trace tr_S sends the class of a closed point z to [κ(z):F_{q^m}], hence it sends the class of a 0-cycle defined over F_{q^m} to its degree over F_{q^m}. Therefore tr_S(cl(D) cup cl(E)) = D·E, the usual intersection number, which is a rational number. In particular beta(x,x) = D^2 and beta(x,ξ) = D·H. Since x ∈ P^2, L(x) = x cup ξ = 0. Applying tr_S gives 0 = tr_S(x cup ξ) = D·H. Let bar(D) be the numerical class of D in Num(S_k) ⊗_Q R. The last equality says that bar(D) is orthogonal to the numerical class bar(H) of H for the intersection pairing on Num(S_k). We now show bar(D) ≠ 0. Suppose bar(D) = 0. The intersection form on NS(S_k) factors through Num(S_k), so D·E = 0 for every E in NS(S_k). View D as an element of NS(S_k) ⊗_Q R. The intersection form on NS(S_k) is the one appearing in lemma_464; its statement defines this form by cup product in H^2_et(S_k,Q_ℓ) followed by the trace normalized by tr(cl(z))=1 for geometric closed points. Applying lemma_464 to the surface S_k over the algebraically closed field k (with ℓ ≠ p = char k) tells us that the R-bilinear extension of this form to NS(S_k) ⊗_Z R is nondegenerate. Since D is orthogonal to every element of NS(S_k), nondegeneracy forces D = 0 in NS(S_k) ⊗_Q R. But the cycle class map NS(S_k) ⊗_Q R -> H^2_et(S_k,Q_ℓ) is the map used to define that form, so cl(D) = 0. This contradicts x = cl(D) ≠ 0. Hence bar(D) ≠ 0. Finally apply lemma_362 to S regarded as a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over the finite field F_{q^m} (replace q in the lemma by q^m), with the same algebraic closure k and with the ample divisor H. It says that the restriction of the intersection pairing on Num(S_k) ⊗_Z R to the orthogonal complement of bar(H) is negative definite. Since bar(D) is a nonzero element of that orthogonal complement, we get bar(D)^2 < 0. But beta(x,x) = D^2 = bar(D)^2. The number D^2 is rational because D is a Q-linear combination of F_{q^m}-rational Cartier divisors and the intersection pairing on integral divisors is integer-valued. Since it is strictly negative, beta(x,x) is the image in Q_ℓ of a negative rational number. This proves the claim.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, and put k=algebraic closure of F_q. Let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample Cartier divisor, let L be cup product with xi, put P^2=ker(L:H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell)->H^4_et(S_k,Q_ell)). Let A be the Q_ell-span in H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) of the cycle classes of F_{q^m}-rational Cartier divisors on S, and let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell). Then beta|_{(A cap P^2) x (A cap P^2)} is nondegenerate.
proof: Let H be the very ample Cartier divisor on S whose cycle class is xi, and write tr for the Poincare duality trace H^4_et(S_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77, tr is an isomorphism and the pairing beta(x,y)=tr(x cup y) on H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) is perfect. Since L(x)=x cup xi, we have beta(x,xi)=tr(L(x)); because tr is an isomorphism, x lies in P^2=ker(L) if and only if beta(x,xi)=0. Let NS_Q = NS(S_k) tensor_Z Q and Num_Q = Num(S_k) tensor_Z Q. Let cl: NS_Q -> H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) be the cycle class map and num: NS_Q -> Num_Q the numerical quotient map. The compatibility of the cycle class map with Poincare duality, which is the definition of the intersection form in the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_464, gives beta(cl(v),cl(w))=v.w for all v,w in NS_Q tensor_Q Q_ell, with the fixed identification of Q_ell(1) with Q_ell; a different nonzero normalization would only multiply this equality by a nonzero scalar. Let V0 be the Q-subspace of NS_Q generated by the classes of Cartier divisors on S defined over F_{q^m}. Put M = V0 tensor_Q Q_ell. By definition of A, A = cl(M). For v in NS_Q, write v.H for the intersection number of v with the class of H. This gives a Q-linear functional f: V0 -> Q. Let V1 = ker(f). Choose a Q-basis e_1,...,e_r of V0 and write f(e_i)=c_i in Q. Then a vector sum a_i e_i in V0 tensor_Q Q_ell has f equal to sum c_i a_i, so the condition v.H=0 is one Q-linear equation; hence M0 := M cap {v in M : v.H = 0} equals V1 tensor_Q Q_ell. For v in M, beta(cl(v),xi)=v.H, so cl(v) lies in A cap P^2 if and only if v.H = 0; hence A cap P^2 = cl(M0). We claim that cl and num are injective on NS_Q tensor_Q Q_ell. By the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_464, the intersection form B on NS(S_k) tensor_Z R is nondegenerate. Hence the Q-form on NS_Q is nondegenerate, and therefore its Q_ell-extension B_l on NS_Q tensor_Q Q_ell is nondegenerate. If cl(v)=0 for some v in NS_Q tensor_Q Q_ell, then B_l(v,w)=beta(cl(v),cl(w))=0 for every w in NS_Q tensor_Q Q_ell, so v=0. If num(v)=0, then B_l(v,w)=0 for every w as well, so v=0. Thus both maps are injective. Let U = num(V1), a Q-subspace of Num_Q. Since num is injective on NS_Q tensor_Q Q_ell, num(M0) = U tensor_Q Q_ell. For every u in U we have u.H = 0, so U tensor_Q R is contained in the orthogonal complement of the class Hbar of H in Num_Q tensor_Q R. Since q^m is again a prime power, we may apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_362 to the surface S over F_{q^m} and the ample divisor H. It says that the intersection form on Num_Q tensor_Q R is negative definite on the orthogonal complement of Hbar. Therefore its restriction to U tensor_Q R is negative definite. Consequently the Q-bilinear form B_U on U is nondegenerate: if u in U were orthogonal to every element of U, then B_U(u,u)=0, contradicting negative definiteness unless u=0. Choose a Q-basis of U; the Gram matrix of B_U has nonzero determinant in Q, so its image in Q_ell is nonzero. Thus the Q_ell-bilinear form B_U_l on U tensor_Q Q_ell is nondegenerate. Finally, for v,w in M0 we have beta(cl(v),cl(w)) = v.w = B_l(v,w) = B_U_l(num(v),num(w)). The map cl identifies M0 with A cap P^2, and the map num identifies M0 with U tensor_Q Q_ell. Under these identifications, the restriction of beta to (A cap P^2) times (A cap P^2) is exactly the nondegenerate form B_U_l. Therefore beta restricted to (A cap P^2) times (A cap P^2) is nondegenerate.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be either 1 or -1, let beta: V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let F be an element of GL_K(V), let c be a nonzero element of K, and suppose beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. Let U be the unique unipotent K-linear endomorphism of V commuting with F such that F U^(-1) is semisimple over an algebraic closure of K. Put G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+epsilon c beta(x,F^(-1)y). Then G(Ux,Uy)=G(x,y) for all x,y in V.
proof:
I have verified all the ingredients. The target is a pure linear-algebra statement: the unipotent part $U$ of a similitude $F$ of a nondegenerate bilinear form is a $\beta$-isometry (this is exactly the proved Jordan-decomposition lemma `eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_554`, applied over an algebraic closure), and because $U$ commutes with $F$ (hence with $F^{-1}$), it is automatically an isometry of $G(x,y)=\beta(x,Fy)+\epsilon c\,\beta(x,F^{-1}y)$.

\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\textbf{Proof.}\\
&\text{Step 1 (base change). Let }K'\text{ be an algebraic closure of }K,\ V'=V\otimes_K K',\ F'=F\otimes 1,\ U'=U\otimes 1,\\
&\text{and extend }\beta\text{ to }\beta':V'\times V'\to K',\ \beta'(\sum x_i\otimes a_i,\sum y_j\otimes b_j)=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\,\beta(x_i,y_j).\\
&\text{The matrix of }\beta'\text{ is the base change of the matrix of }\beta;\text{ since }\beta\text{ is nondegenerate, }\det(\beta)\neq0\in K,\\
&\text{and }K'\text{ is faithfully flat over }K,\ \det(\beta')=\det(\beta)\otimes1\neq0\text{ in }K',\text{ so }\beta'\text{ is nondegenerate.}\\
&\text{Also }\beta'(F'x,F'y)=c\,\beta'(x,y)\text{ for all }x,y\in V',\text{ and }c\neq0.\\[4pt]
&\text{Step 2 (identify the unipotent part). }U\text{ is unipotent, so }U-1\text{ is nilpotent, hence }U'-1\text{ is nilpotent, so }U'\text{ is unipotent.}\\
&\text{Since }U\text{ commutes with }F,\ U'\text{ commutes with }F'.\text{ By hypothesis }FU^{-1}\text{ is semisimple over an algebraic closure of }K;\\
&\text{semisimplicity over an algebraic closure is independent of the choice of such a closure (it is the condition that the}\\
&\text{minimal polynomial over }K\text{ has only distinct irreducible factors), so }FU^{-1}\text{ is semisimple over }K',\text{ i.e. }F'(U')^{-1}\text{ is semisimple.}\\
&\text{Thus }U'\text{ is a unipotent endomorphism commuting with }F'\text{ such that }F'(U')^{-1}\text{ is semisimple, so by the}\\
&\text{uniqueness of the Jordan decomposition of }F',\ U'\text{ is the unipotent part }F_u\text{ of }F'.\\[4pt]
&\text{Step 3 (}U\text{ is a }\beta\text{-isometry). By }eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma\_554\text{ applied to }(K',V',\beta',F'),\\
&\text{with unipotent part }F_u=U',\text{ we get }\beta'(U'x,U'y)=\beta'(x,y)\text{ for all }x,y\in V'.\\
&\text{Restricting to }x,y\in V\subset V',\text{ since }U'x=Ux,\ U'y=Uy\text{ and }\beta'\text{ restricts to }\beta\text{ on }V,\\
&\text{we obtain }\beta(Ux,Uy)=\beta(x,y)\text{ for all }x,y\in V.\tag{$\star$}\\[4pt]
&\text{Step 4 (}U\text{ commutes with }F^{-1}).\text{ From }UF=FU,\text{ multiply on the left by }F^{-1}:\ F^{-1}UF=U;\\
&\text{multiply on the right by }F^{-1}:\ F^{-1}U=UF^{-1}.\\[4pt]
&\text{Step 5 (}U\text{ preserves }G). \text{For }x,y\in V,\\
&\quad G(Ux,Uy)=\beta(Ux,F\,Uy)+\epsilon c\,\beta(Ux,F^{-1}Uy).\\
&\text{Since }U\text{ commutes with }F,\ F\,Uy=UFy;\text{ since }U\text{ commutes with }F^{-1},\ F^{-1}Uy=UF^{-1}y.\text{ Hence}\\
&\quad G(Ux,Uy)=\beta(Ux,UFy)+\epsilon c\,\beta(Ux,UF^{-1}y).\\
&\text{Applying }(\star)\text{ with }(x,\,Fy)\text{ and with }(x,\,F^{-1}y)\text{ (both are elements of }V),\\
&\quad \beta(Ux,UFy)=\beta(x,Fy),\qquad \beta(Ux,UF^{-1}y)=\beta(x,F^{-1}y).\\
&\text{Therefore }G(Ux,Uy)=\beta(x,Fy)+\epsilon c\,\beta(x,F^{-1}y)=G(x,y).\qquad\blacksquare
}

\}
}

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline F_q, let d>=2, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^n=H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell). Fix nonzero elements of Q_ell(1) and Q_ell(-d) to identify the relevant Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, and suppose L^{d-n}:H^n -> H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0<=n<=d. Let P^d=ker(L:H^d -> H^{d+2}) and let beta(x,y)=tr_X(x cup y), where tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->Q_ell is the Poincare duality trace. Then beta restricted to P^d x P^d is nondegenerate.
proof: We apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_542. Its hypotheses match the present statement: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^m} (with d>=2, hence in particular d>=1), xi is the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, L is cup product with xi, and L^{d-n}:H^n -> H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d. Let tr^0_X denote the normalized Poincare duality trace used in that lemma. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_542, for each 0<=r<=d, if P^r = ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r -> H^{2d-r+2}) and beta_r(x,y)=tr^0_X(L^{d-r}x cup y), then beta_r restricts to a perfect pairing on P^r. Take r=d. Then d-r+1=1 and 2d-r+2=d+2, so the P^d in that lemma is exactly ker(L:H^d -> H^{d+2}), which is the P^d in the present statement. Also L^{d-d}=L^0 is the identity on H^d, so beta_d(x,y)=tr^0_X(x cup y). Hence tr^0_X(x cup y) is a perfect pairing on P^d x P^d. Now compare this with the trace tr_X appearing in the target statement. The map tr_X is the Poincare duality trace after the chosen identification Q_ell(-d) with Q_ell, while tr^0_X is the normalized Poincare duality trace. Both are Q_ell-linear isomorphisms H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> Q_ell, so there exists a scalar c in Q_ell^* such that tr_X = c tr^0_X (if the target convention already uses the normalized trace, then c=1). Therefore the target form beta(x,y)=tr_X(x cup y) equals c beta_d(x,y). Multiplication of a bilinear form by a nonzero scalar preserves nondegeneracy: if beta(x,y)=0 for every y, then beta_d(x,y)=0 for every y, so x=0 by perfectness of beta_d; the same argument with the two variables interchanged gives the other side. Thus beta restricted to P^d x P^d is nondegenerate.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be either 1 or -1, let beta: V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let F be an element of GL_K(V), let c be a nonzero element of K, and suppose beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. Put G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+epsilon c beta(x,F^(-1)y). If G(x,x) is nonzero for every nonzero x in V, then F is semisimple on V.

The strategy: take the multiplicative Jordan decomposition $F = F_s F_u = F_u F_s$ with $F_s$ semisimple and $F_u$ unipotent. By `Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_495`, the unipotent part $F_u$ is an isometry of $ eta$. Since $F_u$ commutes with $F$ and $F^{-1}$, it is also an isometry of $G$. Then `eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_585` forces $F_u = \mathrm{id}$ (because $G(x,x)
eq 0$ for all nonzero $x$), so $F = F_s$ is semisimple.

We are given G(x,x) != 0 for every nonzero x in V, and we must show F is semisimple.

Step 1 (Jordan decomposition). Since char K = 0, F has a multiplicative Jordan decomposition F = F_s F_u = F_u F_s, where F_s is semisimple, F_u is unipotent, and F_s, F_u commute. Moreover F_u is a polynomial in F (indeed F_u = exp(N) where N is the nilpotent part of log F, a polynomial in F), so F_u commutes with F and with F^{-1}. In particular F F_u = F_u F and F^{-1} F_u = F_u F^{-1}.

Step 2 (F_u is a beta-isometry). The form beta is nondegenerate, hence perfect. By the lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_495 applied to the perfect bilinear form beta, the similitude F with multiplier c, and its multiplicative Jordan decomposition F = F_s F_u = F_u F_s, the unipotent part F_u is again a similitude of beta with multiplier 1: beta(F_u x, F_u y) = beta(x,y) for all x,y in V.

G(F_u x, F_u y) = beta(x, F y) + epsilon c beta(x, F^{-1} y) = G(x,y).

Take U = F_u: it is unipotent (Step 1) and is a G-isometry (Step 3). The lemma concludes U = id_V, i.e. F_u = id_V.

Step 5 (F is semisimple). Since F = F_s F_u and F_u = id_V, we have F = F_s, which is semisimple by construction of the Jordan decomposition. Therefore F is semisimple on V. This completes the proof."

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1, let k be an algebraic closure of F_q, let d>=2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth geometrically connected very ample Cartier divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, and let i:Y -> X be the closed immersion. Then i^*:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is injective.
proof: Let Q = q^m = p^{am}. Regard X as a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_Q; the given k is also an algebraic closure of F_Q. Let U be the open complement of Y in X. Since Y is a very ample Cartier divisor, it is an effective divisor whose associated line bundle is very ample, hence it is a nonempty effective ample divisor of pure dimension d-1. By the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement, applied to X over F_Q and the smooth ample divisor Y, one has H^j_et,c(U_k, Q_ell) = 0 for every integer j < d. Now apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_357 to X, Y, and U over F_Q. Its hypotheses are satisfied: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension d >= 1, Y is an effective ample divisor over F_Q, smooth of pure dimension d-1, and the compactly supported cohomology groups H^j_et,c(U_k, Q_ell) vanish for all j < d. The conclusion of that lemma is that the restriction map i^*: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) is injective for every integer n with 0 <= n <= d-1. Taking n = d-1 gives the desired injectivity.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, put k=overline F_q, let d>=2 be an even integer, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}. Write H^n=H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell). Fix nonzero elements of Q_ell(1), Q_ell(-d), and Q_ell(d/2) to identify the relevant Tate twists with Q_ell. Let A be the Q_ell-span in H^d of the cycle classes of codimension d/2 cycles on X defined over F_{q^m}. Let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^d, let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^d, and put G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+q^{md} beta(x,F^(-1)y). Then G(x,y)=2 q^{md/2} beta(x,y) for all x,y in A.
proof: Let Q=q^m and r=d/2. Since d is even, r is an integer at least 1, and Q is a prime power. Put k=overline F_q=overline F_Q and regard X as a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over F_Q. Let sigma:k->k be the automorphism c->c^Q. The q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F in the statement is the pullback (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^*. Using the fixed nonzero element of Q_l(1), and hence of Q_l(r), we identify Q_l(r) with Q_l, so the cycle classes of codimension-r cycles on X defined over F_Q lie in H^d=H^{2r}(X_k,Q_l). The subspace A is their Q_l-span. Apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_503 with its base prime power replaced by Q, its extension degree replaced by 1, and its j replaced by r. In that lemma the space V is the Q_l-span in H^{2r}(X_k,Q_l) of the cycle classes of all codimension-r cycles on X_{F_Q}; but X_{F_Q}=X, so V=A. The lemma says that the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius, which is exactly the above F, acts on V=A as multiplication by Q^r=q^{mr}=q^{md/2}. Thus for every y in A, F y = lambda y, where lambda=q^{md/2} is a nonzero element of Q_l. The operator F is an automorphism of H^d because it is the pullback by the automorphism id_{X_k} x Spec sigma of X_k, whose inverse is the pullback by id_{X_k} x Spec sigma_inv, where sigma_inv is the inverse automorphism of sigma; hence F^{-1} exists. Since F restricted to A is lambda times the identity and lambda is nonzero, for every y in A we have F^{-1}y=lambda^{-1}y. The pairing beta is the Poincare duality pairing H^d x H^d -> Q_l(-d) followed by the fixed isomorphism Q_l(-d)->Q_l, so it is Q_l-bilinear. Therefore, for x,y in A, G(x,y)=beta(x,F y)+q^{md} beta(x,F^{-1}y)=beta(x,lambda y)+q^{md} beta(x,lambda^{-1}y)=(lambda+q^{md}lambda^{-1})beta(x,y). Since lambda=q^{md/2}, we have q^{md}lambda^{-1}=q^{md}q^{-md/2}=q^{md/2}=lambda. Consequently G(x,y)=2lambda beta(x,y)=2q^{md/2}beta(x,y), as required.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be a prime, let m>=1, and put k=algebraic closure of F_q. Let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample Cartier divisor, let L be cup product with xi, put P^2=ker(L:H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell)->H^4_et(S_k,Q_ell)), let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, let beta be the Poincare duality pairing on H^2_et(S_k,Q_ell) given by cup product followed by the Poincare trace, and set G(x,y)=beta(x,Fy)+q^{2m} beta(x,F^{-1}y). If x in P^2 is a nonzero Q-linear combination of the cycle classes of F_{q^m}-rational Cartier divisors on S, then G(x,x) != 0.

  "proof": "Let H be the very ample Cartier divisor whose class is xi, and let h be its class in NS(S_k). Write F for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. First compute G(x,x). Apply the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_314 with the base prime power q' = q^m, codimension j = 1, and with its internal parameter m equal to 1. For every F_{q^m}-rational divisor D on S, one has F(cl(D)) = q^m cl(D). Since x is a Q-linear combination of such classes, F(x) = q^m x. Because F is an automorphism of H^2(S_k,Q_l), applying F^{-1} gives F^{-1}(x) = q^{-m}x. Hence G(x,x) = beta(x,q^m x) + q^{2m} beta(x,q^{-m} x) = q^m beta(x,x) + q^m beta(x,x) = 2q^m beta(x,x). The scalar 2q^m is nonzero in Q_l, so it is enough to prove that beta(x,x) is nonzero. Next remove the dependence on the normalization of the Poincare trace. Let tr0 be the standard Poincare trace on H^4(S_k,Q_l) normalized by tr0(cl(z)) = 1 for every closed point z of S_k, and put beta0(u,v) = tr0(u cup v). Since H^4(S_k,Q_l) is one-dimensional, the trace used in the statement is lambda tr0 for some lambda in Q_l^times, and therefore beta = lambda beta0 and G = lambda G0. Thus it suffices to prove that G0(x,x) is nonzero, equivalently that beta0(x,x) is nonzero. Now use the Hodge index theorem. Let c: NS(S_k) tensor Q -> H^2(S_k,Q_l) be the cycle class map. By the assumption on x, x = c(w) for some w in NS(S_k) tensor Q. If w were zero, then x would be zero, so w is nonzero. Since x is in P^2, we have x cup xi = 0, hence beta0(x,xi) = 0. Under the fixed identification of Tate twists, xi = c(h), and by the definition of the intersection form used in lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_464, beta0(c(a),c(b)) is the usual intersection number a

·b for a,b in NS(S_k) tensor Q. Therefore beta0(x,xi)=beta0(c(w),c(h))=w·h=0. Let B be the R-bilinear extension of the intersection form on NS(S_k) tensor R. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_464, B is nondegenerate of signature (1,rho-1), where rho is the rank of NS(S_k). The class h is the class of the very ample divisor H. Since very ample implies ample, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_272 with the base prime power q^m to the ample divisor H; it shows that the degree of cl(H)^2 is the image in Q_l of a positive rational number. Under the standard trace tr0, beta0(c(h),c(h)) is the image in Q_l of the usual self-intersection number H^2, so the real number B(h,h) is positive. We now show that the orthogonal complement h^perp = { y in NS(S_k) tensor R : B(y,h)=0 } is negative definite. If rho=1, nondegeneracy and B(h,h)>0 imply h spans the positive line, so h^perp=0, and the claim is vacuous. Assume rho>=2. Choose an orthogonal basis e_0,...,e_{rho-1} of NS(S_k) tensor R with B(e_0,e_0)=1 and B(e_i,e_i)=-1 for i>=1. Write h=a_0 e_0 + v, v=sum_{i>=1} a_i e_i. From B(h,h)=a_0^2 - sum_{i>=1} a_i^2 >0, we get a_0^2 > sum_{i>=1} a_i^2, in particular a_0 !=0. Let y=b_0 e_0 + u, u=sum_{i>=1} b_i e_i, be orthogonal to h. Then 0=B(y,h)=a_0 b_0 - sum_{i>=1} a_i b_i, so a_0 b_0 = sum_{i>=1} a_i b_i. If u=0, then sum_{i>=1} a_i b_i=0, hence a_0 b_0=0 and b_0=0, so y=0. If u !=0, Cauchy-Schwarz on the negative definite subspace spanned by e_1,...,e_{rho-1} gives (sum_{i>=1} a_i b_i)^2 <= (sum_{i>=1} a_i^2)(sum_{i>=1} b_i^2) < a_0^2 sum_{i>=1} b_i^2. Hence b_0^2 = (sum_{i>=1} a_i b_i)^2/a_0^2 < sum_{i>=1} b_i^2, and B(y,y)=b_0^2 - sum_{i>=1} b_i^2 <0. Thus every nonzero y in h^perp has B(y,y)<0. Since w is nonzero and w·h=0, viewing w in NS(S_k) tensor R gives B(w,w)<0. Since beta0(x,x) is the image in Q_l of this negative rational number, beta0(x,x) is nonzero. Consequently G0(x,x)=2q^m beta0(x,x) is nonzero, and therefore G(x,x)=lambda G0(x,x) is nonzero. This proves the lemma."

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let epsilon be either 1 or -1, let beta: V x V -> K be a nondegenerate bilinear form with beta(x,y)=epsilon beta(y,x), let F be an element of GL_K(V), let c be a nonzero element of K, and suppose beta(Fx,Fy)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. Let U be the unique unipotent K-linear endomorphism of V commuting with F such that F U^{-1} is semisimple over an algebraic closure of K. Then beta(Ux,Uy)=beta(x,y) for all x,y in V.
proof:
Let k = algebraic closure of K (fixed), and set W = V \otimes_K k. Extend beta to W by linearity, still denoted beta, so beta(x\otimes a, y\otimes b) = ab beta(x,y). Choose a k-basis of W and let B be the matrix of beta in it, so beta(x,y) = x^T B y for column vectors. Let Fbar = F \otimes_K k. The hypothesis beta(Fx,Fy) = c beta(x,y) extends to all x,y in W:
    (1)  Fbar^T B Fbar = c B.

Jordan-Chevalley decomposition. By hypothesis U is unipotent, commutes with F, and S := F U^{-1} is semisimple over k. Since U commutes with F, US = UFU^{-1} = F = SU, so S and U commute and F = SU is the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition. Over k, Fbar = Sbar Ubar = Ubar Sbar with Sbar = S\otimes k semisimple (diagonalizable over k), Ubar = U\otimes k unipotent, commuting.

Primary decomposition. Let lambda_1,...,lambda_r be the distinct eigenvalues of Fbar in k, and for each j let n_j >= 1 be the size of the largest Jordan block of Fbar for lambda_j. Put W_j := ker(Fbar - lambda_j I)^{n_j}. The minimal polynomial of Fbar is prod_j (T - lambda_j)^{n_j} with pairwise coprime factors, so
    (2)  W = direct sum_{j=1}^r W_j.
Each W_j is Fbar-invariant. Since Ubar commutes with Fbar it commutes with every polynomial in Fbar, in particular with (Fbar - lambda_j I)^{n_j}; hence Ubar and Ubar^{-1} (unipotent, hence invertible) preserve each W_j. Thus Sbar = Fbar Ubar^{-1} also preserves each W_j. Write Fbar|_{W_j} = lambda_j I + N_j with N_j := (Fbar - lambda_j I)|_{W_j} nilpotent, N_j^{n_j} = 0.

Step 1: Sbar|_{W_j} = lambda_j I. Fix j and set R := Ubar^{-1}|_{W_j}. Since Ubar is unipotent, R is unipotent (if Ubar = I + N with N nilpotent then Ubar^{-1} = I - N + N^2 - ... is unipotent). Also R commutes with N_j: R commutes with Ubar, and Ubar commutes with Fbar, hence with N_j. Now
    Sbar|_{W_j} = Fbar|_{W_j} R = (lambda_j I + N_j) R = lambda_j I + T,   T := lambda_j(R - I) + N_j R.
We prove T is nilpotent. (i) lambda_j(R - I) is nilpotent: R - I is nilpotent (R unipotent) and lambda_j != 0 is a scalar. (ii) N_j R is nilpotent: N_j is nilpotent and commutes with R, so (N_j R)^m = N_j^m R^m = 0 for m >= n_j. (iii) lambda_j(R - I) and N_j R commute: from RN_j = N_j R we get (R - I)(N_j R) = RN_jR - N_jR = N_jR^2 - N_jR = (N_jR)(R - I). (iv) A sum of two commuting nilpotent endomorphisms is nilpotent: if A^p = B^q = 0 and AB = BA, then (A+B)^{p+q} = sum_{i=0}^{p+q} binom(p+q,i) A^i B^{p+q-i} = 0, since in every summand either i >= p (A^i = 0) or p+q-i >= q (B^{p+q-i} = 0). Hence T is nilpotent, so Sbar|_{W_j} = lambda_j I + (nilpotent); its only eigenvalue is lambda_j.
It remains that Sbar|_{W_j} is semisimple. Write W = direct sum_mu E_mu with E_mu = ker(Sbar - mu I) (Sbar diagonalizable over k). For mu != nu the projection p_mu = prod_{nu != mu} (Sbar - nu I)/(mu - nu) is a polynomial in Sbar, so p_mu(W_j) subseteq W_j (W_j is Sbar-invariant). Hence W_j = direct sum_mu (W_j \cap E_mu) and Sbar|_{W_j} is diagonalizable. A diagonalizable endomorphism with a single eigenvalue lambda_j equals lambda_j I. Therefore
    (3)  Sbar|_{W_j} = lambda_j I,   Ubar|_{W_j} = (Sbar|_{W_j})^{-1} Fbar|_{W_j} = I + (1/lambda_j) N_j.

Step 2 (block lemma): Ubar|_{W_j}^T B_{j\ell} Ubar|_{W_\ell} = B_{j\ell} for all j, \ell, where B_{j\ell} is the block of B representing (x,y) -> beta(x,y) for x in W_j, y in W_\ell (beta(x,y) = x^T B_{j\ell} y).
First, by induction on n >= 0, Fbar^{nT} B Fbar^n = c^n B: n=0 is the identity, and Fbar^{(n+1)T} B Fbar^{n+1} = Fbar^T (Fbar^{nT} B Fbar^n) Fbar = Fbar^T (c^n B) Fbar = c^n Fbar^T B Fbar = c^{n+1} B, using (1). Since Fbar preserves each W_m, restricting to the (j,\ell) block gives
    (4)  (Fbar|_{W_j})^{nT} B_{j\ell} (Fbar|_{W_\ell})^n = c^n B_{j\ell}.
Now (Fbar|_{W_j})^n = (lambda_j I + N_j)^n = sum_{a=0}^{n_j} binom(n,a) lambda_j^{n-a} N_j^a (the sum is effectively a < n_j since N_j^{n_j} = 0), and similarly (Fbar|_{W_\ell})^n = sum_{b=0}^{n_\ell} binom(n,b) lambda_\ell^{n-b} N_\ell^b. Substituting into (4):
    sum_{a,b} binom(n,a) binom(n,b) lambda_j^{n-a} lambda_\ell^{n-b} (N_j^a)^T B_{j\ell} N_\ell^b = c^n B_{j\ell}   for all n >= 0.
Define C_{a,b} := (N_j^a)^T B_{j\ell} N_\ell^b and D_{a,b} := lambda_j^{-a} lambda_\ell^{-b} C_{a,b}. Dividing by (lambda_j lambda_\ell)^n != 0:
    (5)  sum_{a,b} binom(n,a) binom(n,b) D_{a,b} = (c/(lambda_j lambda_\ell))^n B_{j\ell}   for all n >= 0.
Set r := c/(lambda_j lambda_\ell) and P(n) := sum_{a,b} binom(n,a) binom(n,b) D_{a,b}. Each binom(n,a) binom(n,b) is a polynomial in n of degree a+b, with a <= n_j, b <= n_\ell, so P is a polynomial of degree at most d := n_j + n_\ell. Equation (5) says P(n) = r^n B_{j\ell} for all integers n >= 0.
Apply the (d+1)-st forward difference Delta^{d+1} (Delta f(n) = f(n+1) - f(n)). On one hand Delta^{d+1} P(n) = 0 since deg P <= d. On the other hand, by induction Delta^m r^n = (r-1)^m r^n for all m >= 0 (base: Delta r^n = r^{n+1} - r^n = (r-1) r^n), so Delta^{d+1}(r^n B_{j\ell}) = (r-1)^{d+1} r^n B_{j\ell}. Since (5) holds for all n >= 0 and Delta^{d+1} only samples values at arguments >= n >= 0, we get
    (6)  (r - 1)^{d+1} r^n B_{j\ell} = 0   for all n >= 0.
If r != 1: then (r-1)^{d+1} != 0 and r^n != 0, so (6) forces B_{j\ell} = 0, and Ubar|_{W_j}^T B_{j\ell} Ubar|_{W_\ell} = 0 = B_{j\ell}.
If r = 1: then (5) reads P(n) = B_{j\ell} for all n >= 0. Evaluate at n = 1 (binom(1,a) = 0 for a >= 2):
    P(1) = D_{0,0} + D_{1,0} + D_{0,1} + D_{1,1} = B_{j\ell}.
Since D_{0,0} = C_{0,0} = B_{j\ell}, this gives D_{1,0} + D_{0,1} + D_{1,1} = 0. Using (3),
    Ubar|_{W_j}^T B_{j\ell} Ubar|_{W_\ell} = (I + N_j^T/lambda_j) B_{j\ell} (I + N_\ell/lambda_\ell) = C_{0,0} + C_{0,1}/lambda_\ell + C_{1,0}/lambda_j + C_{1,1}/(lambda_j lambda_\ell) = D_{0,0} + D_{0,1} + D_{1,0} + D_{1,1} = B_{j\ell}.
Thus in both cases Ubar|_{W_j}^T B_{j\ell} Ubar|_{W_\ell} = B_{j\ell} for every pair (j,\ell).

Step 3 (conclusion over k). By the direct-sum decomposition (2), Ubar^T B Ubar = B is equivalent to the collection of block identities just proved. Hence Ubar^T B Ubar = B, i.e.
    (7)  beta(Ubar x, Ubar y) = beta(x, y)   for all x, y in W.

Step 4 (descent to K). Identify V with V \otimes_K K subseteq W. For x, y in V, Ubar x = (U \otimes k) x = Ux, and beta(Ubar x, Ubar y) = beta(Ux, Uy) \cdot 1_k while beta(x,y) = beta(x,y) \cdot 1_k (beta was extended by linearity). Equation (7) gives beta(Ux, Uy) \cdot 1_k = beta(x, y) \cdot 1_k in k. The inclusion K -> k is injective, so beta(Ux, Uy) = beta(x, y) in K.
This holds for all x, y in V, completing the proof. (Note: the parameter epsilon and the nondegeneracy of beta are not needed; the similarity relation (1) suffices.)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1, let k be an algebraic closure of F_q, let d>=2, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}, let Y be a smooth geometrically connected very ample Cartier divisor on X defined over F_{q^m}, and let i:Y -> X be the closed immersion. Then i^*:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0 <= n <= d-2.
proof: Set q0 = q^m = p^(am). Since F_{q0} is a finite extension of F_q, the given algebraic closure k of F_q is also an algebraic closure of F_{q0}; we use the same k for both base fields. Regard X and Y as defined over F_{q0}. By the meaning of a very ample Cartier divisor, there is a very ample line bundle L on X, defined over F_{q0}, and a nonzero section s in H^0(X,L) whose zero scheme is exactly Y; equivalently one may take L = O_X(Y) and the canonical section. As Y is a Cartier divisor in the smooth variety X of pure dimension d, Y is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1. Put U for the open complement of Y in X. Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_435_geometrically_connected with its parameter q replaced by q0. Its hypotheses are satisfied: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=1 over F_{q0}, L is a very ample line bundle over F_{q0}, s is a nonzero section, and its zero scheme Y is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1. Hence H^j_c(U_k, Q_ell) = 0 for every integer j < d. Apply lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type to the closed immersion Y_k -> X_k with open complement U_k. It gives a long exact sequence ... H^n_c(U_k, Q_ell) -> H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) -> H^{n+1}_c(U_k, Q_ell) -> ... in which the middle map is i^*. Now fix n with 0 <= n <= d-2. Then n < d and n+1 <= d-1 < d. By the vanishing just obtained, H^n_c(U_k, Q_ell) = 0 and H^{n+1}_c(U_k, Q_ell) = 0. The relevant exact segment is therefore 0 -> H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) -> 0. Exactness at H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) implies the kernel of i^* is zero; exactness at H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell) implies the image of i^* is all of H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell). Thus i^* is an isomorphism. Since n was arbitrary in the stated range, the lemma is proved.
